headline: Schwab blocks outside AI agents from client accounts and directs clients to Charley
body: Charles Schwab said on October 15 that it is blocking outside AI agents that use client login credentials or browser automation, and is directing clients to its own assistant, Charley, while allowing them to use ChatGPT and other large language models for stock trades. CEO Rick Wurster said an agent trying to log in on behalf of a client is “not safe”.
note: Cash is part of the story too. Tim Welsh of Nexus Strategies says Schwab has an incentive to keep that business, and Schwab reported nearly $3.48 billion in net interest revenue in the third quarter.
correction: Body said Schwab blocks outside agents from accessing accounts; the source says it blocks agents that use client login credentials or browser automation and still allows ChatGPT and other LLMs for trades. Tense fixed.

evidence.text: Schwab is specifically preventing AI agents from using clients' login credentials or browser automation to access its systems.
A little over a month after Meta released its Muse AI assistant capable of performing financial and other tasks, Charles Schwab says it's blocking outside agents from accessing its clients' accounts.
Instead, Schwab is directing clients to its own fledgling AI assistant, Charley, while also allowing them to use ChatGPT and other large language models for stock trades and other transactions.
And there's one way we think is not safe, and that's just an agent coming to our site and trying to log in on behalf of a client.
In an earnings call Thursday, Schwab CEO Rick Wurster portrayed the decision to block outside AI agents as necessary for protecting client data.
Tim Welsh, the founder of the consulting firm Nexus Strategies, said the concerns about protecting clients' data are no doubt real.
Schwab, he said, clearly has an incentive to prevent AI agents from infringing on business it wants to keep for itself.
Schwab, for instance, reported on Thursday that it made nearly $3.48 billion in net interest revenue in the third quarter, much of it on nearly $493 billion held in cash-sweeps accounts.
